newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS - Peso drop seen driving up Philippine inflation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Peso drop seen driving up Philippine inflation.

text.p: The de facto devaluation of the peso would drive up prices of Philippine food and petroleum products but inflation would remain within manageable limits, government officials and economists said on Friday.

"Definitely this (effective devaluation of peso) is inflationary...the magnitude of which depends on the final amount of depreciation after the market calms," said economist Luz Lorenzo of Peregrine Securities.
After Friday's surprise announcement by the Central Bank saying it would allow the currency to move in a wider range, the peso plunged 11.5 percent to 29.45 per dollar.
Several government officials immediately issued statements to allay fears that a weaker peso would drive up inflation.
"We expect a slight uptick in inflation. I'm sure it will be tolerable. I am very confident that it will not be double digit," Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson said.
Economic and Planning Secretary Cielito Habito said there would be no substantial impact on inflation provided there was no "opportunistic overpricing by merchants and enterprises."
"The government will remain vigilant against those who would use the exchange rate movement as an excuse for unwarranted price increases," he said.
Trade and Industry Secretary Cesar Bautista said he had met business leaders who had assured him that prices would not rise.

"Because of fierce competition among manufacturers to win consumer favour, the business leaders believed their members will think twice and be cautious about changing their marketing and pricing policies," he said.
The Philippines' policy of keeping the peso in a firm band had so far kept inflation under control with the figure going down to 4.8 percent in June from the year-ago 9.8 percent.
Economists said inflation was now bound to rise but opinions on its extent differed.
"The fact that the Philippines is a major importer of coal, oil and refined products, there is an inflationary effect," James Brown of Merrill Lynch in Sydney said.
"The prices of electricity and products are now deregulated. Any increase in peso terms can be passed onto consumers," he added.
Philippine oil refiners said they expected the average price of local petroleum products to rise by as much as 60 centavos per litre due to a weak peso.
Assuming an exchange rate of 29 pesos per dollar compared to the previous 26.4, the landed cost of crude will increase by 40 centavos per litre, an executive at an oil firm said.

"With roughly 20 billion litres a year consumption, this will cost the oil firms eight billion pesos, how can the industry absorb that? But we have to see at what level the peso would stabilise," he said.
Philippine flour mills shelved plans on Friday to place orders for wheat.

"With the peso pegged at 29.45 pesos, the price of a 25-kg bag of flour in the domestic market has to be adjusted to (raised by) between 26 and 30 pesos per bag to reflect additional cost that we have to pay for the wheat and its freight," one trader said.
